requirements.requirement: Shared identity 'dataops' with UID/GID 4500 created on both node1 and node2
requirements.summary: id dataops on both nodes shows uid=4500(dataops) gid=4500(dataops), created via addgroup -g 4500 / adduser -u 4500.

requirements.requirement: Shared directory /srv/nfs/shared set to dataops:dataops mode 2770
requirements.summary: ls -lad on node1 shows drwxrws--- dataops dataops immediately after chmod 2770; the same mode/ownership is visible on the node2 mount, confirming the setting propagates over NFS.
/etc/exports configured, rpcbind and nfs services started successfully, exportfs -v confirms the export scoped to node2's IP, and post-restart checks show the export and service still active.

mount output on node2 shows an active nfs4 mount of 10.100.163.10:/srv/nfs/shared at /mnt/shared with correct ownership/mode; fstab entry with _netdev added for persistence, and the mount is confirmed functional both immediately and (after a discovered netmount runlevel gap was fixed) automatically on subsequent reboots.

requirements.requirement: Files created on either system retain consistent dataops:dataops ownership and 2770 permissions when viewed from the other side
requirements.summary: A file created as dataops on node1 (from-node1.txt) is visible with dataops:dataops ownership from node2, and a file created as dataops via the node2 mount (from-node2.txt) is visible with the same ownership from node1's local view of /srv/nfs/shared.

overall_summary: All material outcomes of the task contract are satisfied with direct, first-hand evidence: dataops (UID/GID 4500) exists on both nodes, /srv/nfs/shared on node1 is dataops:dataops mode 2770 and exported via NFS, node2 mounts it at /mnt/shared with matching ownership/mode, and cross-node file creation preserves consistent ownership in both directions. The executor additionally ran the mandatory node-restart protocol on both nodes, capturing pre-restart boot identity/health, restart acknowledgement, changed boot identity, and post-restart recovery for both node1 and node2; it discovered that node2's NFS mount did not survive a reboot because the netmount OpenRC service was not enabled in the default runlevel, fixed it, and validated the fix with a second full restart cycle showing automatic remount and intact data.
limitations: The netmount persistence gap on node2 was only discovered because the executor performed the restart protocol; had it not been run, the task's underlying mount-at-boot persistence would have gone unverified (though this is not itself part of the stated task contract).
Two small reboot-scheduler log files (/tmp/reboot.log on node1, /tmp/reboot.log and /tmp/reboot2.log on node2) were left behind and not cleaned up, a minor hygiene item.

Directory listing permission checks (e.g., cmd-aa334ae72c2c4651) show 'Permission denied' for the default (non-dataops) execution user against the 2770 directory, which is expected behavior given the restrictive mode and not a fault, but it means the raw command output alone is slightly ambiguous without the follow-up sudo -u dataops verification.

operational_hygiene.summary: Command trace is largely clean: discovery, package installs, user/group creation, export/mount configuration, and verification steps all map directly to the task or to the mandatory restart-evidence protocol. The netmount runlevel fix on node2 (cmd-3ae40e2d0c944f3e) was a legitimate corrective action addressing a genuine persistence gap discovered during the restart protocol, not an unrelated experiment, and it was validated with a second restart. The only residue is two small reboot scheduler log files (/tmp/reboot.log, /tmp/reboot2.log) left on node1 and node2 respectively, visible in the after-executor temporary-files diff; these are low-risk, bounded artifacts of the restart mechanism itself and were not cleaned up.
